finding: §3.4.6 assigns unit ids "in ascending first-hunk-start order within a round", but first-hunk-start is a line number and the ordering names no file component and no tiebreak. A PR touching three files whose first hunks start at lines 5, 10 and 10 has no defined id assignment: two implementations will interleave files differently and will break the 10/10 tie differently. Unit ids are referenced by mapping.ndjson, coverage cells, findings and prompts, so the whole round's state hangs off an order that §2.1.1 requires to be reproducible. §8.3.3 defines a total order with explicit tiebreaks for exactly this reason; §3.4.6 does not.
suggestion: Make the order total and file-aware, mirroring §8.3.3: order units by first hunk's file path ascending, then first hunk's start line ascending, then side (LEFT before RIGHT); state that ids are assigned u1..uN over that order.

finding: §3.4.6 requires "a normalised hash of its changed lines called the unit hash", but §1.4 normalises a *text* and nothing says how the changed lines are assembled into one. Unspecified: the order (hunk order vs line order), the separator, whether the diff's `+`/`-` prefixes are included, whether file paths or line numbers participate, and — given §3.4.1's two-case definition — whether a unit containing both an add-only hunk and a delete-only hunk hashes RIGHT and LEFT lines into one text and in what order. A tester cannot write "the unit hash of this diff is X". This is not cosmetic: §4.5.5 stores the unit hash on every cell and §10.2.2 makes completeness depend on a cell having been filled for the unit's *current* hash, so two implementations disagree on when coverage is invalidated. §8.3.3 explicitly refuses this laxness for the payload hash ("never over a JSON serialisation whose field order or spacing is unspecified") and §9.2 defines the anchor hash's pre-image precisely; the unit hash is held to neither standard.
suggestion: Define the pre-image explicitly, e.g.: the unit's changed lines per §3.4.1, taken in ascending hunk order and ascending line order within a hunk, content only with the diff marker stripped, joined by LF, then normalised and hashed per §1.4.

finding: §3.7 characterises `cr brief` as read-only with respect to judgement, permits it only to "compute and persist the derived inputs of §3.3 through §3.6", and states "It is safe to run at any point in a round." §9.3.3 and §9.3.4 now make `cr brief` the sole round-advancing mutator: it increments the round index, rewrites the recorded head, moves every `draft` and `queued` record to the terminal state `stale`, and clears `mapping.ndjson`. Discarding a round's unposted findings is neither a derived input of §3.3–§3.6 nor safe to run at any point, and §9.1's table names `cr brief` as the actor for that transition. An implementer reading §3.7 first will build a pure reader.
suggestion: Replace §3.7's "It is safe to run at any point in a round" with a pointer to §9.3.3, and extend §3.7's permitted-writes clause to cover the round index, the recorded head, and the §9.3.4 staling. Alternatively move the round advance to an explicit `cr round start` and leave `cr brief` pure.

finding: §4.5.6 says `cr cells record` "replaces the current round's cells and is keyed by (unit, role)" — two incompatible write modes in one sentence: wholesale replacement of the round's cell set, or upsert on the (unit, role) key. §4.6.5 makes the difference destructive rather than academic: the review runs in two mandated passes, the intent role returns in pass 1 and the other three roles in pass 2. Under the replacement reading the pass-2 `cr cells record` erases every intent cell, and §10.2.2 (a complete row for every active role) then becomes unsatisfiable unless the agent happens to re-submit pass-1 cells inside the pass-2 file — which nothing requires. Under the upsert reading a cell the agent withdraws can never be removed.
suggestion: Pick one and say it: either "upserts by (unit, role), leaving cells for other roles untouched; a cell is removed only by recording it with `na`", or "replaces the round's cells for the roles named in the file". Given §4.6.5's two passes, per-role upsert is the only mode that works; state it there too.

finding: §5.2.5 gives a run `passed: true` on `exit_code` 0 whenever `tests_failed` is not derivable or is zero, with no guard on `tests_run` being zero. §5.4.4 then gates a `failed` gap probe on "its baseline passed per §5.2.5". A gap probe's baseline runs the probe's filter on code that does not yet contain the supplied test file, so whenever the filter names that test — the ordinary case — the baseline selects zero tests, exits 0, and is recorded `passed: true`. The guard added to close round 5's "gap probe has no baseline guard" therefore passes vacuously in exactly the situation it was written for: a repository with a pre-existing suite failure still yields a `probed` grade at severity `high`. §5.3.4 rung 3 and §5.4.3 rung 3 guard the probe run against zero executed tests; nothing guards the baseline.
suggestion: Add to §5.2.5: "A run whose executed test count is known and equals zero, or whose executed count is undeterminable, MUST have `passed: false`." Or state in §5.4.4 that the baseline must have `tests_run` greater than zero to support the finding.

finding: §5.3.2 says `cr probe run --kind mutation` "MUST apply the mutation, run the tests, revert the mutation, and record the result", but nothing defines the behaviour when the supplied patch fails to apply. §5.3.4's ladder is declared "total over every run" and its rung 2 covers only "the runner could not be started, or exited on a signal" — the gap ladder's rung 2 does cover a bad input ("the supplied test failed to compile or load → error"), the mutation ladder's does not. Two testers write contradictory tests: one asserts exit 4 with no probe record, the other asserts a probe record with result `error`. Worse, a third reading — apply best-effort, then run — walks straight down to rung 5 (`failed count is zero`) → `no-test-failed`, which §5.3.5 treats as *proof of the gap* whenever the baseline passed. A mutation that never landed then manufactures the strongest grade in the system on unmutated code.
suggestion: Add a rung or a precondition: a mutation patch that does not apply cleanly MUST abort with exit code 3 (or be recorded with result `error`) before any test run, and MUST NOT be able to reach rungs 3-6. State explicitly that the tests are run only after a verified-clean application.

finding: `target` is now required on every probe record and is validated only for existence ("validated as §6.2.3 validates a citation" — path exists, line in range). Nothing anywhere compares it to the record it grades. §6.2's table grants `probed` to a record "referenc[ing] a probe whose head matches and whose result supports the claim per §5.3 and §5.4"; §5.4.4 binds a gap probe to the record by requiring the finding's `claim` field to name the claim the test asserts, but §5.3.5 imposes no locational or claim binding at all for a mutation probe. So one `no-test-failed` mutation probe at u1 can grade a finding anchored in u9 as `probed`, and §5.5.2 ("at most one probe") does not prevent it — it only limits the count. A tester cannot decide whether `cr record` accepts such a record, and the answer determines whether the strongest grade — the one that licenses an assertion rather than a question — can be pointed at arbitrary code.
suggestion: Require that a probe may grade a record only when the probe's `target` resolves inside that record's unit (or matches its anchor path and falls within the unit's hunk ranges), and require `cr record` to reject a `probed` claim that fails the check with exit code 1, naming the record and the probe.

finding: A legitimate mechanical rule hit buys the assertion register that §6.3 denies to reasoning, and the purchase is configurable per repository. Trace: §2.6 lets any per-repo rule file carry `detect` and `kind: finding`. §2.6.1.3 records a hit as a citation with `origin: rule`. §6.2's `cited` row exempts an `origin: rule` citation from the 'lies outside the record's own unit' test, so a hit on the very line being commented on grades the record `cited`. §6.3.1's forcing applies only to `argued`, so `kind: finding` survives and the record posts as an assertion. But §2.6.1.5 states outright that 'Detection MUST report hits, never verdicts' — the regex establishes only that a string matched, and the judgement that it is a real violation is the agent's, which is exactly what `argued` means. The 'outside its own unit' condition exists to stop 'I assert X about this line, citing this line'; the rule-origin exemption reintroduces that shape and blesses it with assertion register. §2.7 declares the argued forcing unconfigurable and unreadable from any layer, yet a five-line rule file in `~/.cr/repos/<owner>/<repo>/rules/` confers assertion register on any pattern its author cares to write. §2.6.2.4 already applies the right humility to the *replacement* half of a rule ('cr cannot establish that a generated replacement compiles… MUST be labelled as machine generated'); the *detection* half gets none.
suggestion: Drop the `origin: rule` exemption from §6.2's `cited` row so a rule-origin citation qualifies under the same 'outside the record's own unit' test as an agent citation — a rule hit that is the finding's own line is self-reference and grades `argued`, which is the honest register for 'a pattern matched and the agent believes it matters'. If the exemption is kept deliberately, then extend §8.1.6's weak-provenance disclosure to it: a record whose only qualifying citation has `origin: rule` MUST name the rule and state in the posted body that the evidence is a mechanical pattern match, mirroring §2.6.2.4's machine-generated label.

finding: §8.1 assembles a posted comment from three sources — the `cr`-owned label line of §8.1.4, the agent-written body of §8.1.2, and the `cr`-owned citation block of §8.1.7 — and never defines the boundary between them, which leaves two load-bearing rules unenforceable. (a) §8.1.7 requires the citation block to be 'regenerated at render time and at post time', 'NOT be editable through the draft', and 'any edit to it MUST be discarded rather than posted'. §7.1.1 defines exactly one marker per record, the opening HTML comment; nothing delimits where the agent body ends and the `cr` block begins. §7.1.5 makes comparison against `rendered.json` 'the only observable basis for detecting a user edit', and §7.1.6 requires regeneration to 'preserve bodies for records whose body differs from `rendered.json`' — so a differing body is preserved wholesale, which is the opposite of discarding the edit. With no delimiter, an agent that appends a fabricated `path:line` line to the block produces text the reader parses as tool-generated and `cr` cannot separate from its own, which is the precise failure §8.1.7 was written to close. (b) §8.1.5 refuses to post a `kind=question` 'body' with no `?`, and justifies itself as the only thing that makes §6.3's forcing visible to the reader. §8.1.3 and §8.1.5 say 'body', §8.1.7 says 'the agent-written body', §8.1.4 says 'comment'. Whether the `?` test runs before or after the two `cr`-owned blocks are attached decides whether it means anything: run against the assembled comment, `cr` can satisfy its own honesty check with its own text, and an argued finding whose prose reads as a flat assertion posts because the label line happened to end in `?`.
suggestion: Define the boundary explicitly in §8.1: a posted comment is the §8.1.4 label line, then the agent body, then the §8.1.7 citation block, with the two `cr`-owned regions delimited by fixed `cr`-owned HTML comment markers that §8.1.3 forbids a body from containing. State that `rendered.json` stores the agent-body region alone, so §7.1.5 and §7.1.6 compare and preserve only that region and everything outside it is regenerated rather than read back. State in §8.1.5 that the `?` test runs over the agent-body region alone, excluding the §8.1.4 label and the §8.1.7 block.

finding: §8.1.2 lets the agent rewrite a block's body "entirely" by editing draft.md (§7.1.2 repeats "free-form Markdown that the user may rewrite entirely"), while §8.1.4 requires `cr` to prepend a fixed `cr`-owned label line to every question and §8.1.7 requires `cr` to append a `cr`-owned citation block that "MUST be regenerated at render time and at post time, MUST NOT be editable through the draft, and any edit to it MUST be discarded". §7.1.1 defines only a leading HTML-comment marker per record; no delimiter separates the `cr`-owned regions from the agent-owned body. `cr` therefore cannot tell where the body ends and its own text begins after a rewrite. A tester cannot write either test: "an edit to the citation block is discarded" has no observable boundary, and "the label is prepended" is not idempotent — one implementation re-prepends and produces two labels, another strips a heuristically matched prefix and can eat an agent sentence. §8.1.4 states this line is the sole channel by which §6.3's forcing reaches the reader, so losing or doubling it is not a formatting nit.
suggestion: Give both regions machine-readable delimiters, e.g. `<!-- cr:label -->` … `<!-- /cr:label -->` and `<!-- cr:citations -->` … `<!-- /cr:citations -->`, define the body as exactly the text outside them, and state that `cr` strips and regenerates the delimited regions at render and post time so the operation is idempotent.

finding: §3.4.6 justifies round-scoped unit ids "because §9.3.3 recomputes the unit set", but §9.3.3 says only that `cr brief` increments the round index and stores the new head. No section requires the diff to be re-ingested or units re-clustered at a new head. §3.7 makes persisting units a MAY, not a MUST. So round 2 can legally proceed against round 1's `units.ndjson`: unit ids and unit hashes never update, §10.2.2's "filled for that unit's current unit hash" compares against a hash from the old head, and §4.6.1 emits prompts carrying hunks that no longer exist.
suggestion: Add to §9.3.4: "On that increment `cr` MUST re-ingest the diff and recompute `units.ndjson` per §3.4 at the new head before any other command reads it, and MUST clear `mapping.ndjson` and the round's coverage cells." Then §3.4.6's cross-reference is true.

finding: §9.3.5 declares "Per-PR files are append-only", but four other requirements truncate or mutate those same files: §9.3.4 clears `mapping.ndjson`, §3.3.1 replaces `claims.ndjson` "for the current round" and clears `mapping.ndjson`, §4.1.6 replaces `mapping.ndjson`, §4.1.7 re-derives `intent-gaps.ndjson` on every mapping write, §4.1.8 stamps `set_aside_note` onto an existing gap entry, and §6.1's computed `state`, `disposition`, `duplicate_of` and `thread_id` change on every §9.1 transition of a record already written to `findings.ndjson`. Append-only would require writing a second generation of each record, and §9.3.5's only read rule — "read only the current round's records" — does not disambiguate two generations carrying the same round and head, so `cr draft`, §6.4 dedup and §10.2.4 would all see each record twice. I cannot write the storage layer without knowing which discipline governs.
suggestion: Restrict "append-only" to what it was meant to protect — history across rounds — and say so: earlier rounds' records are never rewritten, while the current round's `claims`, `mapping`, `cells` and `intent-gaps` files are rewritten in place and a record in `findings.ndjson` is updated in place. Alternatively keep strict append-only and define the disambiguator (last record wins per id, and per generation counter for the replaced files).

finding: §9.3.5's "Per-PR files are append-only" contradicts four other MUSTs, one of them the line directly above it. §9.3.4 requires `mapping.ndjson` to be cleared; §3.3.1 requires `cr claims record` to replace `claims.ndjson` and clear `mapping.ndjson`; §4.1.6 requires `cr map record` to replace `mapping.ndjson`; §4.5.6 requires `cr cells record` to replace the current round's cells. §9.3.3 also requires `meta.json`'s round index and recorded head to be mutated in place, and §2.3 lists `rounds/<n>/rendered.json` and `posted.json`, none of which are append-only. An implementer cannot satisfy both readings and the two produce different histories.
suggestion: Scope the rule: "`findings.ndjson`, `probes.ndjson`, `runs.ndjson`, `transitions.ndjson`, `posted-index.ndjson`, and `waivers.ndjson` are append-only. `claims.ndjson`, `units.ndjson`, `mapping.ndjson`, `intent-gaps.ndjson`, and `coverage.ndjson` are replaced per round. `meta.json` and the `rounds/<n>/` files are written in place."

finding: §9.3.6 says a finding matching the posted index "MUST be dropped before drafting". By then the record already exists in `findings.ndjson` in state `draft` (written by `cr record`). §9.1's transition table is declared exhaustive and offers `draft` only `duplicate`, `suppressed`, `queued`, and `stale`, so a posted-index drop has no legal destination state and the record stays `draft` forever. §10.2.4 then blocks completeness permanently for any PR that reaches a second round. §6.4.4 avoids exactly this for waivers by requiring the dropped finding never be written to `findings.ndjson` at all; §9.3.6 has no equivalent.
suggestion: Apply the posted-index drop at the same point and with the same rule as §6.4.4: the finding is not written to `findings.ndjson`, only the count reaches the round summary. Change "dropped before drafting" to match §6.4.4's wording.

finding: §9.3.6 requires a finding matching the posted index to be "counted in the round summary", but §10.3 enumerates a closed list — raised, deduplicated, suppressed by thread, waived, forced to question, drafted, posted, discarded `not-here`, discarded `wrong`, the comment count, the probe cap state, and the payload hash — with no counter for posted-index drops. Folding them into `waived` would corrupt §7.4's waiver accounting and §7.3's statistics, since a posted-index drop carries no disposition and is not a triage decision.
suggestion: Add "already posted" to §10.3's list of counts, and state that these drops are excluded from the waiver count and from `triage.ndjson`.

finding: §9.3.6 requires a posted-index drop to be 'counted in the round summary', but no section provides the slot and no rule keeps the count visible. §10.3's enumeration is closed and specific — raised, deduplicated, suppressed by thread, waived, forced to question, drafted, posted, discarded `not-here`, discarded `wrong` — and contains no entry for records dropped by the posted index. §10.1.6 reports 'Waivers applied and duplicates suppressed in the current round' and likewise omits it, so `cr status` never shows it either. §11.1's list of disclosures `--quiet` MUST NOT suppress enumerates the axes, probe cap, forcing counts, waiver and duplicate counts, sandbox recreation, stale round, and comment cap — and omits it, so the one suppression that silences a concern across rounds is the one a quiet run may hide. The same omission applies to §4.1.8's set-aside claims. A suppression the reviewer cannot see is a suppression they cannot audit, which is the honesty half of the round-5 repair left undone.
suggestion: Add 'dropped as already posted per §9.3.6' to §10.3's enumeration, add it to §10.1.6's coverage report line alongside waivers and duplicates, and add both it and §4.1.8's set-aside count to §11.1's always-printed list.

finding: §2.3.3 requires "every record in claims.ndjson, units.ndjson, **mapping.ndjson**, findings.ndjson, probes.ndjson, runs.ndjson, intent-gaps.ndjson, and coverage.ndjson" to carry `head` and `round`, but §4.1.6 defines a mapping line as "one `{claim, unit}` pair per line" — two fields, neither of them `head` or `round`. Nothing says whether the agent must supply them (in which case §4.1.6's schema is wrong and `cr map record` must reject a bare pair) or `cr` stamps them (in which case they are computed fields, and §6.1.4's list of fields the agent may not write does not cover them). The same silence applies to §4.5.5's cell schema, which names "the head it was filled against" but no round. A tester cannot decide whether `{"claim":"X#c1","unit":"u1"}` is accepted or rejected with exit code 1.
suggestion: State that `cr` stamps `head` and `round` on mapping and cell records at write time, mark them computed so §6.1.4's prohibition covers them, and align §4.1.6's and §4.5.5's field lists with §2.3.3.

finding: `tests.probe_path_template`'s default is given as `<root of the first tests.globs entry>/cr_probe_<probe-id><ext>`, but `<ext>` is defined nowhere — not in §2.4, not in §5.4. It could be the extension of the agent-supplied test file, a fixed per-profile extension, or derived from `tests.globs`. Nor is the placeholder vocabulary of a user-supplied template stated: whether `<probe-id>` is mandatory, and what happens when a template omits it (every gap probe then targets one path, and §5.4.2's "An existing file at that path MUST abort with exit code 4" fires on the second probe of a round). A tester cannot compute the path the file lands at, which is the one thing §5.4.2 and §5.1.6 both depend on.
suggestion: Define `<ext>` (e.g. the extension of the file passed to `--test`), list the legal placeholders, and require a template to contain `<probe-id>` — rejecting one that does not with exit code 3, naming the profile.

finding: §2.6.1.6 appends three different event kinds — hits, records, and dismissals — to `rule-stats.ndjson` with one field list ("the rule id, the matched `path` and `line`, the round, and the head") and no discriminator naming which kind an entry is. Two requirements need the distinction and cannot get it: §6.2.5 stamps `origin: rule` only when the file "holds a **hit** for the same head with the same rule id and the same path and line", and §2.6.3.4 reports a rule as dead when it "produced no hit and no record" — a rule whose only entries are dismissals would count as live under any reading that cannot separate them.
suggestion: Add a required `event` field to the §2.6.1.6 entry with the closed vocabulary `hit`, `record`, `dismissal`, and add the record id to `record` and `dismissal` entries so a dismissal can be traced back.

finding: §2.6.1.6 requires "every hit, record, and dismissal" to be appended to `rule-stats.ndjson` "with the rule id, the matched `path` and `line`, the round, and the head" — three different event kinds written into one file with no field that distinguishes them. Two consumers need the distinction and cannot compute it: §6.2.5 stamps `origin: rule` only when the file "holds a **hit**" for the same head, rule id, path and line (a dismissal at the same coordinates would satisfy the stated key just as well), and §2.6.3.4 reports rules that "produced no hit and no record", a query that is undefined when hits and records are indistinguishable. A tester cannot construct the fixture that separates the two cases.
suggestion: Add a required `event` field to the `rule-stats.ndjson` schema with the closed vocabulary `hit`, `record`, `dismissal`, and make §6.2.5's match require `event: hit`.

finding: §3.4.1 defines a changed line in two coordinate spaces — RIGHT for hunks that add lines, LEFT for hunks that add none — and says so explicitly ("Line numbers below are RIGHT-side for the first case and LEFT-side for the second"). §3.4.4 then measures adjacency as "the gap between the last changed line of one and the first changed line of the next" within the same file. When a delete-only hunk sits next to an add-bearing hunk, that subtraction crosses the two spaces: the numbers differ by the cumulative line delta of every preceding hunk in the file, and the gap can be negative. This is a common shape (a refactor that deletes a block and adds a replacement below it), and two testers will write contradictory expectations for whether the two hunks cluster.
suggestion: Fix one coordinate space for adjacency — e.g. map a delete-only hunk's LEFT range onto its RIGHT-side insertion point before measuring the gap — and state that the gap is computed in that space.

finding: §4.1.7 derives `intent-gaps.ndjson` "mechanically" on each successful `cr map record`, and §4.1.8 stamps `set_aside_note` onto a gap entry. Nothing says whether a re-run of `cr map record` — which §4.1.6 permits, since it "MUST replace mapping.ndjson" — preserves an existing `set_aside_note` for a claim that is still unmapped. Read as full mechanical re-derivation it is wiped; read as a merge it survives. §10.2.3 makes exactly that stamp the difference between a blocked and a complete round, so the two readings produce opposite completeness verdicts from the same command sequence. The same gap exists for `cr claims record`, which §3.3.1 says clears `mapping.ndjson` while saying nothing about `intent-gaps.ndjson`, leaving it stale against the new claim set.
suggestion: State that re-derivation preserves `set_aside_note` for any claim id that still has a gap entry and drops it otherwise, and that `cr claims record` clears `intent-gaps.ndjson` along with `mapping.ndjson`.

finding: §4.1.7 re-derives `intent-gaps.ndjson` mechanically on **each** successful `cr map record`, and §4.1.8 stamps `set_aside_note` onto an entry in that same file. Since §4.1.6 lets the agent re-record the mapping any number of times within a round, a second `cr map record` regenerates the gap entries and silently discards every `set_aside_note` stamped before it — which re-blocks completeness under §10.2.3 with no message, and forces the reviewer to redo a judgement `cr` is explicitly forbidden from making itself.
suggestion: State in §4.1.7 that re-derivation preserves `set_aside_note` for any claim that is still unmapped, and drops it only for a claim that has become mapped. Alternatively store set-asides in their own file keyed by claim id and have the derivation join against it.

finding: The only thing that makes an unimplemented claim block completeness is clearable by the party it constrains, and the clearing need never be disclosed. §10.2.3 says a claim carrying an unimplemented-claim entry 'MUST block completeness until it is either mapped, or set aside through `cr claims set-aside`', and calls this 'the only thing that makes an unimplemented claim block'. §4.1.8's entire precondition is 'after checking the note exists for the PR's issue key'. §3.6.1 lets `cr note <ISSUE-KEY> "<text>" --source <source>` append a note with arbitrary body and any of the five sources of §3.6.3, and §2.1 makes the agent the process driver — so the agent can write the note and consume it in the next call, converting 'a stated requirement was never implemented' into 'complete' with no human in the path. §10.2's closing paragraph is careful to require that a complete verdict be printed together with the disabled and unavailable axes, 'because completeness across three axes is not completeness across four' — the identical argument applies to a set-aside claim, and no rule requires the verdict to name one. P6 says coverage is proven; here it is asserted by a note the asserting party wrote.
suggestion: Require §10.2's complete verdict to enumerate every set-aside claim with its claim id, note id, and the note's `source`, on the same footing as the disabled and unavailable axes, so a round is never reported complete without naming what was set aside and on whose word. Record the note's `source` and timestamp on the gap entry at `cr claims set-aside` time so a note authored during the same round is distinguishable from one that predates it.

finding: §4.5.1's new definition — "A **role** is active when its axis is active, its `profiles` list is empty or names the resolved profile, and §4.6.4 did not report it skipped" — closes on a term that is never defined. §4.6.4 says only "A role whose prerequisites are unmet MUST be reported as skipped with its reason"; a role's prerequisites appear nowhere in §2.5's schema or anywhere else, so the third clause either restates the first two or names an unknown third condition. The active-role set is the denominator of §10.2.2's completeness check and the rejection criterion of §4.5.6, so a tester cannot construct the case "a role that is skipped but whose axis is active" and cannot pin the completeness verdict.
suggestion: Either drop the third clause and define §4.6.4's skip report as the *output* of the first two conditions, or enumerate a role's prerequisites explicitly in §2.5 and have §4.6.4 report against that list.

finding: §4.6.5 gates the second pass on whether "a mapping exists for the current round and head", but the only observable is `mapping.ndjson`, which §9.3.4 clears at the start of a round and §4.1.6 replaces. A legitimately empty mapping — the agent judged that no unit implements any claim, which §4.1.3 treats as a normal outcome — is byte-identical to a never-recorded one, so `cr review` would refuse the remaining axes with exit code 4 forever and the round could not proceed.
suggestion: Record the fact rather than infer it from file contents: have `cr map record` set a `mapping_recorded` marker (round and head) on `meta.json`, and define §4.6.5's gate against that marker so an empty mapping is a valid answer.

finding: §4.6.5 refuses the non-intent axes with exit code 4 "until a mapping exists for the current round and head", but §4.1.6 requires `cr map record` to replace `mapping.ndjson` and §9.3.4 requires it to be cleared on a new round. A legitimately empty mapping — every claim unimplemented, or a PR that implements nothing the issue states — is byte-identical to a cleared file, so `cr` cannot tell "recorded, and it is empty" from "not yet recorded" and the second pass is refused forever. This is a plausible review, not a corner case: it is precisely the PR §4.1.3 exists to describe.
suggestion: Record the fact of mapping rather than inferring it from file contents: have `cr map record` stamp `mapping_round` and `mapping_head` on `meta.json`, and make §4.6.5's gate read those. Accepting a zero-line mapping file explicitly is then unambiguous.

finding: §5.2.3 requires a run that exceeds `tests.timeout_seconds` to be "killed and recorded as `timeout`", but the run record of §5.2.4 has no field that can hold that: it carries `id`, `head`, `filter`, `exit_code`, `duration_ms`, `tests_run`, `tests_failed`, `output_tail` and `passed` only. A killed process yields some exit code, so `passed: false` is all that survives, and a timed-out baseline becomes indistinguishable from a failing one — which matters because §5.3.5 and §5.4.4 gate `probed` on `baseline.passed`. Only the probe record (§5.5) has a `result` field, and a plain `cr test` run is not a probe.
suggestion: Add a `result` or `timed_out` field to the §5.2.4 run record, with a value vocabulary that at least separates `ok`, `failed`, `error` and `timeout`, and define `passed` (§5.2.5) as false for anything other than `ok`.

finding: §5.5's `baseline` is "Id of the run record (§5.2.4) at the same head whose filter equals this probe's" — a definite article over a set that §5.2.2 does not make singular. Only the unfiltered baseline is pinned to "once per head"; a filtered baseline is recorded per filtered probe, so several run records can share a head and a filter, and `cr test <pr> --filter <expr>` can be invoked directly any number of times. When two such runs disagree (one `passed: true`, one `passed: false` from a flaky or order-dependent suite), the choice between them decides whether §5.3.5 and §5.4.4 grant a `probed` grade. Two testers write contradictory tests: newest matching run vs first vs "abort on ambiguity".
suggestion: State the selection rule — e.g. the most recently recorded run record at the same head with an equal filter — or require the filtered baseline to be recorded once per (head, filter) exactly as the unfiltered one is, and reuse it.

finding: `baseline` is now required on every probe record and is defined as "Id of the run record (§5.2.4) at the same head whose filter equals this probe's", but nothing says who supplies it. Neither §5.3.2's nor §5.4.2's command signature has a `--baseline` flag, §6.1.4's computed-field rule covers records and not probes, and §5.2 places no uniqueness constraint on run records: `cr test` may be run repeatedly at one head with one filter, so several run records can satisfy the definite article. With a flaky suite the choice between them decides whether a `probed` grade is available.
suggestion: State in §5.5 that `cr` selects the baseline itself and that it MUST be the most recent matching run record at the current head, recording an error with exit code 4 when none exists rather than running one implicitly.

finding: `baseline` is now required on every probe record and must name a run record at the same head with the same filter, but no command owns creating it. §5.2.2 states the requirement in the passive voice ("A baseline run with no filter MUST be recorded once per head"; "A filtered probe MUST additionally record a filtered baseline") without naming an actor, and §5.3.2/§5.4.2's `cr probe run` invocations do not mention it. So I cannot tell whether `cr probe run` must abort with exit 4 when no matching run record exists, or must run the baseline itself — and if the latter, whether those implicit suite runs count against `probe.max_per_round` (§5.6.4) and how a filtered probe's two runs interact with the §5.6.1 lock.
suggestion: State the actor in §5.5 or §5.2.2: e.g. "`cr probe run` MUST locate a run record at the current head whose filter equals the probe's, and MUST execute and record one when none exists; baseline runs do not count against `probe.max_per_round`." If the intent is the opposite, say `cr probe run` aborts with exit code 4 naming the `cr test` invocation required.

finding: §6.4.1 dedups on `(anchor.path, anchor.line, class)` — the end line only — while every other identity in the spec now treats the anchor as a range: §9.2 requires `start_line` and hashes `start_line`..`line`, §7.1.1's marker carries `start_line`, §8.3.3 orders and hashes on `start_line`, and §7.4.1 keys a waiver on the hash of the anchored lines. Two records anchored to different ranges that happen to end on the same line are therefore collapsed as duplicates, and §7.4.1's claim that the waiver key "match[es] the class-based identity of §6.4.1" does not hold: the surviving representative's waiver covers a different span than the record that was suppressed, so the suppressed one returns in the next round.
suggestion: Make §6.4.1 key on `(anchor.path, anchor.start_line, anchor.line, class)`, or on `(anchor.path, class, anchor.content_hash)` so it is literally the waiver key of §7.4.1 minus the scope, and drop or correct the correspondence sentence in §7.4.1.

finding: §7.1.1's marker carries `id`, `kind`, `path`, `start_line`, `line`, `severity`, `grade`, and `disposition`, but not `side`. §7.2's marker table says `path`, `start_line`, `line` are "Re-validated per §6.1.2", and §6.1.2 resolves `side: RIGHT` against the head and `side: LEFT` against the merge base. Without `side` in the marker, `cr` cannot know which of the two to re-validate an edited anchor against, and the reviewer editing a deletion comment cannot see that they are addressing a removed line. §8.3.3's payload ordering and per-comment pre-image both include `side`, so it is load-bearing at post time too.
suggestion: Add `side` to the §7.1.1 marker field list and to §7.2's marker table as immutable (like `id`), so re-validation has a defined target and a LEFT record is visible as such in the draft.

finding: §7.4.1's round-5 repair removed the rule id from the waiver key, which leaves §7.4.6's prefix widening both unscoped and permanent. §7.4.6 permits widening 'a waiver for a record produced by a rule' to a path prefix, but with the key now `(anchor.path, class, normalised hash of the anchored lines)` nothing on the waiver identifies which rule produced it — §7.4.5 records the disposition and §7.4.9 the round, PR, head, and reason, and neither records a rule id. A widened waiver therefore suppresses a whole class over a path prefix regardless of producer, silencing agent-authored findings of that class as well. Worse, a prefix necessarily spans many files and lines, so a widened waiver cannot carry the anchored-line hash — which voids §7.4.2's stated guarantee that the key 'stops suppressing once that code changes — which is exactly when the judgement behind the waiver should be revisited'. §7.4.6 thus creates the one waiver shape with no revisit trigger, silently and repository-wide, and it duplicates a mechanism the rule corpus already provides: §2.6's `exempt` field is defined as 'Paths excluded, for legacy areas', the exact stated purpose of §7.4.6.
suggestion: Delete §7.4.6 and point legacy-area exemption at the rule's `exempt` field per §2.6, which is declarative, inspectable through `cr rules list`, and scoped to the rule that owns it. If a widened waiver is kept, require it to record the rule id, restrict its effect to records carrying that rule id, and give it an explicit expiry in rounds so §7.4.2's revisit property is not lost.

finding: Two pieces of text are declared `cr`-owned and uneditable inside a file whose whole point is that the human edits it, with no delimiter defined for either: §8.1.4's question label line (prepended to every `kind=question` comment) and §8.1.7's citation block (appended beneath the body, "MUST NOT be editable through the draft, and any edit to it MUST be discarded"). §7.1.1 defines only an opening marker for a block and §7.1.2 says the body "MUST be free-form Markdown that the user may rewrite entirely", so when `cr draft`/`cr post` read `draft.md` back there is no mechanical way to tell where the agent's body ends and the `cr`-owned text begins — which is exactly what §7.1.6's "preserve bodies that differ from `rendered.json`" and §8.1.7's "discard the edit" both depend on. It is also unstated whether the label line appears in `draft.md` and in `rendered.json` at all, or is added only when the payload is built.
suggestion: Give the `cr`-owned regions explicit HTML-comment delimiters in §7.1.1 (e.g. `<!-- cr:citations -->` … `<!-- /cr:citations -->`), state that everything between them is stripped before the body comparison of §7.1.6 and regenerated afterwards, and say explicitly whether §8.1.4's label is rendered into the draft or injected at payload-build time.

finding: §9.3.2 refuses only to "draft, post, or probe" when the current head differs from the recorded head. `cr record`, `cr claims record`, `cr map record`, and `cr cells record` are unlisted and therefore permitted during a mismatch. §6.2.3 requires citations to be resolved "against the current head", while §6.1's `head` field is "Head SHA the record was produced against" — so a record written during a mismatch is graded against a head its anchor, unit, and hunks were never produced against, and §5.5.3's same-head rule for probes has no counterpart for citations.
suggestion: Extend §9.3.2 to refuse every command that writes per-PR judgement state — record, claims record, map record, cells record — with exit code 4 until `cr brief` advances the round, leaving only the read-only commands and `cr post --reconcile` exempt.

finding: §9.3.6 says a finding matching the posted index "MUST be dropped before drafting", but by drafting time the record already exists in `findings.ndjson` in state `draft` (it was written by `cr record`). §9.1's transition table is declared exhaustive and offers no edge out of `draft` other than `queued`, `duplicate`, `suppressed`, or `stale`, so a dropped record is stuck in `draft` and §10.2.4 ("No record of the current round remains in `draft` or `queued`") can never hold — the round can never be complete. §6.4.4 solves exactly this for waivers by saying the dropped finding is never written at all; §9.3.6 carries no such clause. §9.3.6 also requires the drop to be "counted in the round summary", yet §10.3's enumeration of summary counts has no entry for it.
suggestion: Mirror §6.4.4: apply the posted-index check at `cr record` time, before the record is written, so no record ever exists in a state §9.1 does not define. Add the count to §10.3's list (e.g. "already posted") alongside "waived".

finding: §9.3.5 and §9.3.6 contradict each other on whether the posted index is readable at all. §9.3.5 states that per-PR files are append-only, that 'every record carries `round` and `head`', that 'A command MUST read only the current round's records; earlier rounds are history', and then names the exceptions: 'Waivers per §7.4 and the context store per §3.6 apply across rounds.' `posted-index.ndjson` is a per-PR file listed in §2.3 and is not among the named exceptions, yet §9.3.6 exists solely to act across rounds — 'so a later round never re-asserts a concern already sent' — and a later round exists only because §9.3.3 incremented the index on a head change. Read literally, every entry the index holds was written in an earlier round and is therefore invisible, and §9.3.6 never fires. §2.3.3's list of files whose records must carry `head` and `round` also omits `posted-index.ndjson`, so §9.3.5's blanket claim about per-PR records is inaccurate as well, leaving no principled way to decide which reading governs.
suggestion: Extend §9.3.5's exception sentence to name the posted index: 'Waivers per §7.4, the context store per §3.6, and the posted index per §9.3.6 apply across rounds.' State in §9.3.6 that an entry carries the round and head it was posted at for provenance while matching is head-independent, and either add `posted-index.ndjson` to §2.3.3 or narrow §2.3.3's claim to the files it lists.

finding: §9.3.6's posted-index drop leaves a record in a state §9.1 does not define, and the round can then never complete. §6.4.4 solved this same problem for waivers with an explicit clause — 'A dropped finding MUST NOT be written to `findings.ndjson` at all, so no record ever exists in a state §9.1 does not define; only the count reaches the round summary' — and §9.3.6 copies the drop behaviour without the safeguard. It says only 'dropped before drafting', which places the drop after `cr record` has written the record in state `draft`. §9.1's transition table admits `draft` → `duplicate`/`suppressed` (`cr record`), `draft` → `queued` (`cr draft`), and `draft`/`queued` → `stale` (`cr brief` on a new head); there is no transition for a posted-index drop, and §9.1 declares the table exhaustive with anything unlisted rejected at exit code 4. The record therefore stays in `draft`, and §10.2.4 requires that no record of the current round remain in `draft` or `queued` for the round to be complete — so every round that suppresses even one already-posted concern is permanently incomplete.
suggestion: Mirror §6.4.4 verbatim in §9.3.6: a finding matching a posted-index entry MUST NOT be written to `findings.ndjson` at all, so no record exists in an undefined state and only the count reaches the round summary. Move the drop to record time alongside the waiver drop so the two suppressions behave identically.

finding: §3.6.1 and §3.6.2 specify `cr note <ISSUE-KEY> "<text>" --source <source>` and `cr answer <pr> <record-id> "<text>" --source <source>`, and §3.6.3 makes the source vocabulary normative. §11's table shows both without `--source`, and neither section says whether the flag is required or what it defaults to.
suggestion: Show `--source <source>` in §11's rows for `cr note` and `cr answer`, and state in §3.6.3 whether it is required or defaults to `other`.

finding: No retention or compaction policy exists for any append-only store. `rule-stats.ndjson` grows with every rule hit across every PR and round of a repository's lifetime, and §6.2.5 scans it positionally on the record-time hot path for every citation of every record. `triage.ndjson` grows the same way and is scanned in full by §7.3.3's per-class rates, and §9.3.5 makes the per-PR files append-only across rounds with no pruning.
suggestion: Either state a retention rule — for example that §6.2.5 reads only entries at the current head and §2.6.3.4 only the last `rules.dead_after` rounds, so older entries may be compacted — or state explicitly that unbounded growth is accepted in v0.1 and name the expected scale.

finding: §3.6.1 and §3.6.2 both show `--source <source>` in the command signature and §3.6.3 fixes the valid values, but neither says whether the flag is required or what an omission yields. §11's table shows both commands without it (`cr note <ISSUE-KEY> <text>`, `cr answer <pr> <record-id> <text>`), implying it is optional with an unstated default. §8.1.6 requires a note-sourced claim's provenance to reach the posted body, so the value is reader-facing, not bookkeeping.
suggestion: State that `--source` is required (exit code 2 when omitted) or give it an explicit default of `other`, and align §11's signatures with §3.6.

finding: §4.6.5 makes `cr review <pr>` refuse the remaining axes with exit code 4 "until a mapping exists for the current round and head". A legitimate mapping can be empty — a PR where the intent role maps no unit to any claim, which §4.1.2 and §4.1.4 explicitly anticipate as the unmapped-unit case. An implementation testing for file presence lets the run proceed; one testing for at least one pair deadlocks the PR with no way out, since §4.6.6's escape hatch applies only when the intent axis is *unavailable*. §4.6.5 is where round 5's deadlock finding already landed once, and the empty-but-valid case is the residue.
suggestion: State that a successful `cr map record` satisfies §4.6.5 regardless of how many pairs it contained, and that the gate tests for a recorded mapping for the current (round, head), not for a non-empty one.

finding: §5.1.6's cleanliness check requires that "no file under the path `tests.probe_path_template` yields for any probe id" exists. Quantifying over "any probe id" is only implementable as a glob with `<probe-id>` treated as a wildcard; an implementation that instead enumerates the ids in `probes.ndjson` misses precisely the case §5.3.3 relies on this check for — `cr` killed before the probe record was written, so the id was never recorded while the artefact remains.
suggestion: State that the check globs the template with `<probe-id>` replaced by a wildcard, so a leftover from a run that produced no record is still detected.

finding: §7.1.4 requires the draft header to list "the comment count against `post.max_comments`, as comments that are not posted." The trailing clause has no readable meaning: it is unclear whether it means questions also consume the cap, that the header counts blocks rather than posted comments, or that the count is advisory until `cr post`.
suggestion: Rewrite as "the number of blocks currently queued against `post.max_comments`, noting that the count is what §1.6.2 will check at post time."

finding: §7.1.4's trailing clause does not parse: "The file MUST open with a summary header listing counts, the coverage state, and the comment count against `post.max_comments`, as comments that are not posted." It is unclear whether "as comments that are not posted" qualifies the counted set (only records that will not be posted?), the header's own lines, or is a leftover from an edit.
suggestion: Rewrite as an explicit list of what the header shows, e.g. "the number of queued comments and the `post.max_comments` cap, so the reviewer sees before triaging whether the round exceeds it per §1.6.2".

finding: §7.1.6 preserves "bodies for records whose body differs from `rendered.json`", without saying whether the comparison is byte-exact or normalised per §1.4. The section immediately above stores "the normalised hash of the whole draft file" and calls it "the only observable basis for detecting a user edit", yet the per-record rule the spec actually operates on compares bodies, and no requirement consumes the whole-file hash. A whitespace-only edit is preserved under one reading and silently regenerated away under the other.
suggestion: State that the per-record comparison is over the normalised body per §1.4, and either name a consumer for the whole-file hash or drop the claim that it is the basis for edit detection.

finding: §9.3.3 defines the round index only differentially — increment iff the current head differs from the recorded head — and never gives its initial value or the behaviour of the first `cr brief` on a PR with no `meta.json` and therefore no recorded head. §2.3's `rounds/<n>/` paths need a defined starting `n`.
suggestion: Add: "On a PR with no recorded state `cr brief` MUST create `meta.json` with round index 1 and the current head; the increment of §9.3.3 applies only thereafter."

finding: §9.3.3 defines when the round index advances but never states its initial value, and §9.3.3's condition ("if and only if the current head differs from the recorded head") makes the very first `cr brief` an increment, since no head is recorded yet. Whether the first round's state lands in `rounds/0/` or `rounds/1/` — and whether the first brief increments 0→1 or starts at 1 — is left open, and §2.3 and §10.3 both address state by `rounds/<n>/`.
suggestion: State that `meta.json`'s round index starts at 0 with no recorded head, so the first `cr brief` yields round 1 and `rounds/1/`.
